title: Polycrisis Resilience: Clean Transition
subtitle: How cleaner energy, industry, transport, homes and farms can reduce interconnected risks and strengthen human survivability
description: How cleaner energy, industry, transport, homes and farms can reduce interconnected risks, strengthen adaptive capacity and support long-term human survivability.
abstract: The global clean transition is often framed as an environmental imperative, but its significance extends far beyond emissions reduction. This report examines the clean transition through the lens of Polycrisis Resilience, arguing that cleaner energy, industry, transportation, household systems, agriculture, and circular resource management can simultaneously reduce multiple interconnected risks while strengthening the adaptive capacities necessary for long-term human survivability. Rather than treating climate change, air pollution, energy insecurity, ecosystem degradation, economic vulnerability, and public health burdens as separate challenges, the report proposes that many share common drivers and can therefore be addressed through coordinated systemic transformation.

The report introduces the central H Heuristics proposition that accelerating the global clean transition can reduce interconnected environmental and socioeconomic risks while enhancing development, technological diffusion, and resilience. It develops a framework organized around six pillars: clean energy, clean industrialization, clean transportation, household energy and pollution reduction, clean agriculture and resource systems, and pollution prevention with circular systems. Together, these pillars illustrate how a single transition can generate multiple benefits across climate mitigation, public health, energy security, economic development, technological convergence, and human wellbeing.

Building on this framework, the report presents the concepts of multi-dimensional resilience, the Clean Transition Resilience Dividend, and a reinforcing feedback loop linking clean-technology adoption, environmental risk reduction, adaptive capacity, and broader resilience outcomes. It further explores how the transition can support economic convergence and technology diffusion in emerging economies, while highlighting barriers such as financing constraints, institutional weakness, and unequal access to capital. Scenario analysis suggests that the greatest resilience gains emerge when clean-transition policies are integrated with investments in adaptation, health, water security, institutional capacity, and human development.

The report concludes that the clean transition should be viewed not only as a strategy for decarbonization, but as a potential mechanism for reducing cascading and compounding crises across multiple domains. While acknowledging significant trade-offs involving critical minerals, affordability, land use, governance, and infrastructure, it argues that a well-designed and inclusive clean transition represents one of the most promising opportunities to increase resilience, reduce human suffering, and strengthen long-term societal survivability in an increasingly interconnected world.
coreProposition: Accelerating the global clean transition can reduce interconnected environmental and socioeconomic risks while strengthening the development and adaptive capacities necessary for long-term human survivability.

keyFindings.title: The pressures are connected, and so are many of the solutions.
keyFindings.text: Climate change, air pollution, water contamination, ecosystem loss, energy insecurity and economic vulnerability reinforce one another. Burning fossil fuels drives climate change and causes much of the outdoor air pollution linked to about 4.9 million deaths a year, while also tying countries to volatile fuel markets.

keyFindings.title: The transition is already well under way, but unevenly.
keyFindings.text: In 2025 renewables generated slightly more of the world's electricity than coal for the first time, and about one in four new cars sold was electric. Yet about 655 million people still lack electricity, about 2 billion lack clean cooking, and Africa receives only about 2% of clean-energy investment.

keyFindings.title: Six pillars carry the transition:
keyFindings.text: clean energy, clean industrialization, clean transportation, household energy and pollution reduction, clean agriculture and resource systems, and pollution prevention and circular systems. Each reduces several pressures at once.

keyFindings.title: One well-designed investment can pay off in seven ways.
keyFindings.text: A solar-plus-storage and grid program can cut emissions and air pollution, power businesses, protect health, diversify energy supply, spread modern technology and support clinics and schools. This is multi-dimensional resilience, though no project delivers every benefit.

keyFindings.title: For emerging economies, the transition is a development strategy.
keyFindings.text: The binding constraint is often the cost of capital, which the IEA finds is more than twice as high for clean projects in emerging and developing economies as in advanced ones.

keyFindings.title: Benefits can reinforce themselves.
keyFindings.text: Cleaner air and cheaper energy improve health and productivity, which strengthen institutions and budgets, which can fund further clean investment. The same loop can run in reverse when pollution and energy poverty trap a country.

keyFindings.title: A broader measure is needed.
keyFindings.text: The proposed Clean Transition Resilience Dividend adds climate, air, health, energy security, economic and resilience gains while removing double-counting. In a hypothetical illustration, gross benefits of 190 fall to 162 after overlap, against a program cost of 100.

keyFindings.title: Decarbonization alone is not enough.
keyFindings.text: In a stylized model, an integrated scenario that pairs the clean transition with adaptation, health, water and institutions ends 2050 with a vulnerability index of 20, against 41 for acceleration alone and 87 for delay.

glossary.definition: The ability of people, institutions and systems to adjust to changing conditions, take advantage of opportunities and cope with consequences.
The spread of failure or stress from one system to others through dependencies.
An economy or process that keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling to reduce waste and the need for new raw materials.
Cooking with fuels and stoves that produce little harmful smoke, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest improved stoves.
The shift from pollution-intensive and inefficient systems toward cleaner energy, industry, transportation, agriculture and infrastructure.
The combined environmental, health, economic and systemic-risk benefits generated by moving to cleaner production and consumption systems (H Heuristics).
A single stress that affects several systems at the same time.
The process by which lower-income economies narrow the gap in income, productivity and capability with wealthier ones.
The minimum return investors require to fund a project. It is higher where risks, real or perceived, are higher.
Small-scale energy systems located near where the energy is used, such as rooftop solar and mini-grids.
Counting the same benefit more than once, for example in both a health category and an economic category.
A circular causal path in which an effect returns to influence its own cause, either reinforcing or dampening it.
Harmful smoke and particles indoors, mainly from cooking and heating with solid fuels or kerosene.
Resilience gained when one intervention reduces risk across several categories at once.
Fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can enter the lungs and bloodstream and are linked to heart and lung disease.
A condition in which crises in multiple systems become causally entangled in ways that worsen overall prospects.

The capacity of individuals, communities, economies, institutions and interconnected systems to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, recover from and reduce the cascading and compounding effects of multiple interconnected crises (H Heuristics).
The spread of a technology from its early adopters to wider users across places and income groups.
A way of combining scores that penalizes low values, such as a geometric mean or a minimum.
